name: Science trivia (easy)
description: 50 easy questions about physics, chemistry, biology, astronomy, the human body, inventions. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
items.explain: Gold is element 79, and its symbol Au comes from the Latin word 'aurum'. Ag is silver.

source.title: Gold - Element information, properties and uses

items.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Na?
items.explain: Na comes from 'natrium', the New Latin name for sodium, an alkali metal in group 1 of the periodic table.

items.question: Which metal has the chemical symbol Fe?
items.explain: Fe comes from 'ferrum', the Latin word for iron.

source.title: Chemical Elements A–Z: Names, Symbols & Atomic Numbers

items.question: Which gas do plants absorb from the air to carry out photosynthesis?
items.explain: Plants use carbon dioxide, water and sunlight to make food, and they release oxygen in the process.

source.title: What is the Carbon Cycle? - NASA Science

items.question: Which green pigment in leaves captures light energy for photosynthesis?
items.explain: Chlorophyll in leaves captures light energy, which is used to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

items.question: How many oxygen atoms are in one molecule of carbon dioxide (CO2)?
items.explain: Carbon dioxide has one carbon atom bonded to two oxygen atoms, which is why it is written CO2.

source.title: What is the Carbon Cycle? - NASA Science

items.question: How many planets are in our solar system?
items.explain: The planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Pluto is classed as a dwarf planet.

items.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
items.explain: Mercury is the planet nearest the Sun, and it is also the smallest planet in the solar system.

items.question: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
items.explain: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.

items.question: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
items.explain: Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

source.title: Planet Facts - Interesting Facts about the Planets

items.question: Which two planets in our solar system have no moons?
items.explain: Mercury and Venus are the only two planets with no moons.

source.title: Our Solar System Information - NASA Science

items.question: How is Pluto classified today?
items.explain: Pluto is one of the five officially recognized dwarf planets, along with Ceres, Haumea, Makemake and Eris.

items.question: Which astronomer made the first detailed telescope observations of Jupiter in 1610 using a small homemade telescope?
items.explain: Galileo Galilei made the first detailed observations of Jupiter in 1610 with a small, homemade telescope.

items.question: How many bones are in the typical adult human skeleton?
items.explain: An adult skeleton has 206 bones. Babies are born with more, and many of them fuse as they grow.

items.question: What are the individual bones that make up the spine called?
items.explain: The spine is made of 33 ring-shaped bones called vertebrae, and it protects the spinal cord.

items.question: Who is credited with patenting the telephone in 1876?
items.explain: Bell received the first patent for the telephone in March 1876.

items.question: Which inventor created the phonograph in 1877, a machine that recorded sound on a rotating cylinder?
items.explain: Thomas Edison invented the phonograph in 1877. It recorded and reproduced sound on a rotating cylinder wrapped in tinfoil.

items.question: What shape is the structure of a DNA molecule?
items.explain: DNA is made of two strands twisted into a double helix, often compared to a twisting ladder or spiral staircase.

items.question: Which two scientists published the double-helix model of DNA in 1953?
items.explain: Watson and Crick proposed in 1953 that DNA is shaped like a double helix.

items.question: What is the chemical formula for water?
items.explain: A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, so its formula is H2O.

items.question: At what temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, does water freeze at sea level?
items.explain: Water freezes at 0°C, which is 32°F.

items.question: At what temperature, in degrees Celsius, does pure water boil at sea level?
items.explain: At sea level, water boils at 100°C, which is 212°F.

items.question: Why does ice float on liquid water?
answers: Ice is more dense than liquid water
Ice contains many large trapped air pockets
Ice is less dense than liquid water
Ice is held up by surface tension alone
items.correct: Ice is less dense than liquid water
items.explain: Ice has an open structure that makes it less dense than liquid water, so it floats.

items.question: Roughly what portion of Earth's surface is covered by water?
items.explain: Water covers about 71% of Earth's surface, and the seas and oceans hold most of it.

items.question: Roughly how much of the human body is made of water?
items.explain: Water makes up roughly 65% of the human body, which is about two-thirds.

source.title: Unusual Properties of Water - Chemistry LibreTexts

items.question: What is the main cause of Earth's ocean tides?
items.explain: The Moon's gravity drives Earth's tides, and the Sun adds a smaller effect.

items.question: Which scientist formulated the three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation?
items.explain: Isaac Newton set out the three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation.

items.question: According to Newton's third law of motion, every action has what?
answers: An equal reaction in the same direction
A weaker reaction after a delay
items.explain: Newton's third law says that when one object pushes on another, the second pushes back with an equal and opposite force.

items.question: What is the name for an object's tendency to resist changes in its state of motion?
items.explain: Newton's first law describes inertia, which is the tendency to keep resting or keep moving unless a force acts.

items.question: What do we call the force of gravity acting on an object's mass?
items.explain: Mass is a property of matter itself, while weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass.

source.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation - Swift Learning Center - NASA

items.question: How many chambers does the human heart have?
items.explain: The heart has four chambers: two atria on top and two ventricles below.

items.question: Which gas does the blood pick up in the lungs?
items.explain: In the lungs, oxygen goes into the blood and carbon dioxide is taken out when we breathe.

items.question: About how big is an adult human heart?
items.explain: The heart is a muscular organ about the size of a fist.

items.question: What are the blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart called?
items.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins carry blood back to it.

items.question: What is the largest artery in the human body?
items.explain: The aorta is the largest artery in the body. It carries blood from the heart to all parts of the body except the lungs.

source.title: Four Chambered Heart Structure And Function - Circulatory System - MCAT Content

items.question: Who made the first successful powered airplane flights, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903?
items.explain: On December 17, 1903, the Wright brothers made the first successful flights of a powered, heavier-than-air machine.

items.question: In which medium does light travel at its highest speed?
items.explain: Light travels slower inside materials such as glass or water, and its highest speed is in a vacuum.

items.question: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
items.explain: The speed of light in a vacuum is about 299,792 km per second, or roughly 186,000 miles per second.

source.title: What Is the Speed of Light?

items.question: Which two planets are classified as ice giants?
items.explain: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, while Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

items.question: About how long is the cycle of the Moon's phases, from one new moon to the next?
items.explain: The Moon's phase cycle takes about 29.5 days, which is roughly one month.

items.question: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon, in July 1969?
items.explain: Neil Armstrong, commander of Apollo 11, was the first to step onto the lunar surface. Buzz Aldrin followed him.

items.question: What type of star is our Sun?
items.explain: NASA describes the Sun as a yellow dwarf star, a hot glowing ball of hydrogen and helium.

items.question: Which two elements make up most of the Sun?
items.explain: The Sun is a huge ball of hydrogen and helium. Nuclear fusion in its core turns hydrogen into helium and powers its heat and light.

items.question: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
items.explain: The Sun is about eight light-minutes from Earth, so its light takes about eight minutes to arrive.

items.question: About how far is the Sun from Earth?
items.explain: The Sun is about 93 million miles (150 million kilometres) from Earth.

items.question: Our Sun and solar system are part of which galaxy?
items.explain: The Sun orbits the center of the Milky Way, carrying the planets and other objects with it.

items.question: What does a light-year measure?
items.explain: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 6 trillion miles.

items.question: What is the largest organ of the human body?
items.explain: Skin is the body's largest organ. Adults carry about 8 pounds of it, covering roughly 22 square feet.

items.question: Which is the largest internal organ in the human body?
items.explain: The liver is the largest solid internal organ. The skin is larger overall but is not internal.

items.question: Which organ acts as the main command center that controls the body's processes?
items.explain: The brain is the body's main control center. It also handles thinking, learning and problem-solving.

source.title: 6 Largest Human Organs: The Amazing Anatomy of Our Body - Largest.org
